summary: The Kuwait Towers, an old covered souq, fine Islamic art museums and Greek ruins on Failaka Island.
overview: Kuwait is a small, flat desert country at the top of the Gulf, and nearly all its people live in and around Kuwait City. Most visitors come on business or a short stopover, and the city fills two or three days well. Its symbol is the Kuwait Towers on the seafront, three slender spires, two of them carrying spheres covered in thousands of blue and green steel discs. The Gulf Road runs past them along the shore, lined with beaches, cafés and families out walking in the cool of the evening.

Souq Al-Mubarakiya, the old covered market, sells dates, spices, perfumes and Bedouin rugs, with cheap kebab and fish restaurants in its alleys. The museums are better than many expect: the Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salem Cultural Centre has halls of natural history, science and space; the Tareq Rajab Museum and the al-Sabah Collection show Islamic art; and Sadu House keeps alive the weaving of the Bedouin. The Grand Mosque gives guided tours. Off the coast, ferries cross to Failaka Island, with remains of Bronze Age and Greek settlements.

Kuwait City is built for cars: most visitors get about by taxi or ride-hailing app, as buses are slow and walking is hard work for much of the year. Alcohol is banned outright, including in hotels, and so is pork; don't bring either in your luggage. Friday and Saturday make up the weekend. Social life happens in malls, seafront cafés and the diwaniya, the evening gathering where men meet at a host's house to talk, a custom at the heart of Kuwaiti life.

seasons.name: Winter
seasons.text: Cool, sunny days around 19°C and chilly nights near 8°C, colder in the open desert, where Kuwaiti families pitch winter camps. Short rainstorms sometimes flood the roads. February brings the Hala February festival and the national holidays.

seasons.name: Spring
seasons.text: Warm, rising from the mid-20s to over 30°C by late April. After a wet winter the desert turns briefly green. Dust storms are frequent, turning the sky yellow-brown for a day at a time.

seasons.name: Summer
seasons.text: Among the hottest places on Earth: above 45°C on most days from June to August, with a hot, dusty north-west wind and still-warm nights in the 30s. Many Kuwaitis spend it abroad, and the city lives in its air-conditioned malls.

seasons.name: Autumn
seasons.text: October is still hot, in the high 30s for much of the month. November is warm and dry, and the season for evenings on the seafront begins.

whenToGo.weather: A dry desert climate of extremes. Summer temperatures above 50°C have been recorded, and the summer wind can bring sand and dust for days. Winters are short and mild by day but cold at night. Rain is scarce, a little over 100 mm in a year, and falls between November and April, sometimes in sudden heavy storms.

festivals.name: Hala February
festivals.text: A month of concerts, shopping promotions, parades and family events, leading up to the national holidays at the end of the month.

festivals.name: National Day and Liberation Day
festivals.text: Back-to-back holidays: National Day, marking the country's independence and the reign of the ruler who brought it, and Liberation Day, the end of the Iraqi occupation in 1991. The Gulf Road fills with flag-waving crowds, decorated cars and fireworks.

festivals.name: Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr
festivals.when: About 11 days earlier each year: in 2027, February into March
festivals.text: Eating, drinking and smoking in public by day are against the law for everyone during the fast, and restaurants open only after sunset, then stay busy late into the night. Eid al-Fitr then closes the month with three or more days off.

festivals.name: Gergean
festivals.when: The middle of Ramadan, so also about 11 days earlier each year: in 2027, in February
festivals.text: On the evening of the 15th day of Ramadan, children in traditional dress go from house to house singing old songs and collecting sweets and nuts in cloth bags. Malls and hotels hold their own Gergean evenings too.

festivals.name: Eid al-Adha
festivals.when: About ten weeks after Ramadan ends: in 2027, in May
festivals.text: A holiday of several days, when many Kuwaitis travel abroad and the airport is at its busiest.

culture.greetings: "As-salamu alaykum" opens most conversations, and "hala" is a friendly hi. Kuwaitis take time over greetings, asking after your health and family before getting down to business. Men shake hands; with a Kuwaiti woman, let her offer her hand first, and a nod with a hand on the heart is fine if she doesn't. Being invited to a diwaniya is a sign of welcome: arrive in the evening, greet the host first, and accept the coffee and tea.
etiquette: Alcohol and pork can't be sold or brought into the country, and being drunk in public is an offence.
During Ramadan, don't eat, drink, smoke or chew gum in public in daylight: the rule applies to visitors too, and is enforced.
Don't photograph government buildings, oil installations, palaces or military sites, and ask before photographing people.
At the Grand Mosque, women are lent an abaya and headscarf, and everyone takes off their shoes at the door.
Eat and pass things with your right hand, and keep the soles of your feet pointed away from others when sitting on the floor.
culture.tipping: Not expected but appreciated. Leave about 10% in restaurants where no service charge appears on the bill, round up taxi fares, and give something to hotel porters and drivers.
culture.dress: Conservative. Both men and women cover their shoulders and knees in public, and tight or see-through clothes draw stares. Women don't need to cover their hair except in mosques. Keep swimwear for hotel beaches and pools. Bring a jacket for winter evenings in the desert.

food.name: Zubaidi
food.text: Silver pomfret, Kuwait's favourite fish, fried or grilled whole and served with rice.

food.name: Murabyan
food.text: Rice cooked with prawns from the Gulf, onions, dried lime and spices: a seaside cousin of the meat and rice dishes found all round the Gulf.

food.name: Mumawwash
food.text: Rice cooked with green mung beans and often dried shrimp or fish, an old dish of the pearl-diving days.

food.name: Gers ogaily
food.text: A light cake flavoured with saffron and cardamom and topped with sesame seeds, served with tea when guests arrive.

food.name: Nikhi
food.text: Boiled chickpeas seasoned with salt, cumin and lemon, eaten as a cheap, warming snack on winter evenings and in Ramadan.

food.name: Gahwa and chai
food.text: Arabic coffee with cardamom, poured in small cups, and sweet black tea are offered at every diwaniya, office and shop. Fresh dates come with both.

phrases.intro: English is spoken in hotels, malls and offices, and by most younger Kuwaitis. In the Kuwaiti way of speaking, a "k" sound often becomes "ch".

items.meaning: How are you? ("What's your news?", to a man)

items.text: Kuwaiti dinar (KD, KWD), divided into 1,000 fils, the highest-valued currency unit in the world. Cards are taken almost everywhere.
Arabic. English is widely used in business and shops, and the large foreign workforce speaks Hindi, Urdu, Malayalam, Tagalog and many other languages.
